claims.text: Substituting a principal element with one having a significantly different atomic radius increases atomic size mismatch.
Increasing atomic size mismatch increases local lattice distortion in single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Greater local lattice distortion impedes dislocation glide.
Greater local lattice distortion leads to higher hardness.
Greater local lattice distortion leads to higher yield strength.
The proposed starting material is an as-processed, single-phase random solid-solution high-entropy alloy.
Varying one principal element while holding processing and microstructural features constant can isolate the effect of atomic size mismatch.
Matching annealing conditions, strain rate, and grain size controls important alternative influences on mechanical properties.
Atomic size differences induce local lattice distortions.
Higher atomic size mismatch alters dislocation core structure.
Higher atomic size mismatch increases lattice friction and dislocation pinning.
Increased dislocation pinning slows dislocation motion and raises resistance to plastic deformation.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have higher hardness than the lower-mismatch baseline.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have higher yield strength than the lower-mismatch baseline.
Greater atomic size mismatch will produce observable dislocation-core modification and impeded glide in TEM or in situ testing.
The proposed behavior is limited to single-phase alloys at moderate temperatures and strain rates without phase transformation or substantial short-range-order evolution.
The hypothesis may not apply to multiphase alloys or conditions that promote diffusion and phase instability.
Dislocation interactions and local chemical ordering may contribute to strength independently of lattice distortion.

contradictions.description: Both fields propose substituting one principal element while keeping the overall composition constant. Elemental substitution necessarily changes chemical composition unless 'overall composition' means only total atomic fraction or another explicitly defined compositional constraint.

The initial state requires a high-entropy alloy, whereas the baseline permits a conventional binary or simplified multicomponent alloy. Such a baseline changes component count and chemical complexity in addition to atomic size mismatch, weakening the claimed controlled comparison.
